claim: Plasmodium vivax is the major cause of human malaria in the Americas.
source: Plasmodium vivax is the major cause of human malaria in the Americas.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about malaria epidemiology in the Americas.

claim: In 2018, Plasmodium vivax infection accounted for 41% of all malaria cases outside of Sub-Saharan Africa, with a total of 6.5 million cases.
source: In 2018, Plasmodium vivax infection accounted for 41% of all malaria cases outside of Sub-Saharan Africa, with a total of 6.5 million cases and more than 2 billion people in 90 countries at risk (World Malaria Reports, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the World Malaria Reports, 2019.

claim: P. vivax elimination will be significantly more difficult than P. falciparum.
source: There are concerns that P. vivax elimination will be significantly more difficult than P. falciparum as the current measures for malaria control are less effective for P. vivax than for Plasmodium falciparum, with the elimination of the former presenting a major challenge in areas that successfully reduced P. falciparum burden.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effectiveness of current malaria control measures.

claim: P. vivax persistence is due to unique biological features including low peripheral parasitaemia and presence of dormant liver stages (hypnozoites).
source: This persistence is due to some unique biological features complicating treatment and elimination, including low peripheral parasitaemia and presence of dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) which relapse weeks or months after blood infection has been cleared.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about P. vivax biology.

claim: P. vivax infection is associated with low peripheral parasitaemia (<2%) as a result of a strict host cell tropism to immature reticulocytes.
source: P. vivax infection is associated with low peripheral parasitaemia (<2%) as a result of a strict host cell tropism to immature reticulocytes (Malleret et al., 2015; Mayor and Alano, 2015) that are exceedingly rare in peripheral blood (<2%) but highly prevalent in the haematopoietic niche of bone marrow (BM) and spleen (Klei et al., 2017; Rhodes et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to scientific literature.

claim: Immature reticulocytes are exceedingly rare in peripheral blood (<2%) but highly prevalent in the haematopoietic niche of bone marrow (BM) and spleen.
source: P. vivax infection is associated with low peripheral parasitaemia (<2%) as a result of a strict host cell tropism to immature reticulocytes (Malleret et al., 2015; Mayor and Alano, 2015) that are exceedingly rare in peripheral blood (<2%) but highly prevalent in the haematopoietic niche of bone marrow (BM) and spleen (Klei et al., 2017; Rhodes et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klei et al., 2017 and Rhodes et al., 2016.

claim: It was generally assumed that peripheral parasitaemia reflects the majority of P. vivax parasites during infection due to limited microvascular adherence in vivo and endothelial cell (EC) binding in vitro.
source: Because of limited microvascular adherence in vivo and endothelial cell (EC) binding in vitro (Lacerda et al., 2012; Valecha et al., 2009), it was generally assumed that peripheral parasitaemia reflects the majority of P. vivax parasites during infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lacerda et al., 2012 and Valecha et al., 2009.

claim: Discrepancy of parasite biomass based on systemic biomarkers such as Plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) compared to peripheral parasitaemia supports existence of a major P. vivax reservoir outside of circulation, particularly in patients with complicated outcomes.
source: However, discrepancy of parasite biomass based on systemic biomarkers such as Plasmodium lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) compared to peripheral parasitaemia supports existence of a major P. vivax reservoir outside of circulation, particularly in patients with complicated outcomes (Barber et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barber et al., 2015.

claim: Late asexual blood stage P. vivax parasites (i.e. schizonts) are capable of cytoadhering to endothelial host receptors.
source: In support of this hypothesis, studies have demonstrated that late asexual blood stage P. vivax parasites (i.e. schizonts) are capable of cytoadhering to endothelial host receptors (Carvalho et al., 2010; De las Salas et al., 2013) and present at reduced abundance compared to the other blood stages in the blood of P. vivax patients (Obaldia et al., 2018; Lopes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carvalho et al., 2010 and De las Salas et al., 2013.

claim: Late asexual blood stage P. vivax parasites present at reduced abundance compared to the other blood stages in the blood of P. vivax patients.
source: In support of this hypothesis, studies have demonstrated that late asexual blood stage P. vivax parasites (i.e. schizonts) are capable of cytoadhering to endothelial host receptors (Carvalho et al., 2010; De las Salas et al., 2013) and present at reduced abundance compared to the other blood stages in the blood of P. vivax patients (Obaldia et al., 2018; Lopes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Obaldia et al., 2018 and Lopes et al., 2014.

claim: In experimentally infected non-human primates (NHPs), a significant enrichment of sexual stages (gametocytes) and schizonts in BM sinusoids and parenchyma has been observed.
source: In experimentally infected non-human primates (NHPs), a significant enrichment of sexual stages (gametocytes) and schizonts in BM sinusoids and parenchyma has been observed (Obaldia et al., 2018), supporting previous evidence from multiple case reports that identified P. vivax in BM and spleen (Yx et al., 2009; Wickramasinghe et al., 1989; Wickramasinghe and Abdalla, 2000; Salutari et al., 1996; Baro et al., 2017; Machado Siqueira et al., 2012; Lacerda et al., 2008; Brito et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Obaldia et al., 2018.

claim: BM and spleen represent the major reservoir of parasite biomass in P. vivax infection.
source: A series of recent studies in acute and chronic human P. vivax infection have meanwhile provided direct evidence that BM and spleen represent the major reservoir of parasite biomass in P. vivax infection (Baro et al., 2017; Brito et al., 2020; Kho et al., 2021a; Kho et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baro et al., 2017; Brito et al., 2020; Kho et al., 2021a; Kho et al., 2021b.

claim: P. vivax parasites can elicit a potent host response, including inflammation and EC activation, and cause severe and fatal manifestations at significantly lower peripheral parasitaemia than P. falciparum.
source: P. vivax parasites can elicit a potent host response, including inflammation and EC activation, and cause severe and fatal manifestations at significantly lower peripheral parasitaemia than the more virulent species, P. falciparum (Barber et al., 2015; Yeo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barber et al., 2015 and Yeo et al., 2010.

claim: The pathogenic mechanisms underlying alterations in host homeostasis and their relationship with P. vivax biomass are not fully understood.
source: However, the pathogenic mechanisms underlying these alterations in host homeostasis and their relationship with P. vivax biomass are not fully understood (Lacerda et al., 2011; Naing and Whittaker, 2018; Rodriguez-Morales et al., 2005; Tangpukdee et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The study cohort included 79 adult patients with confirmed P. vivax infection and 34 age- and sex-matched uninfected healthy donors.
source: We included 79 adult patients (median age of 36 years) with confirmed P. vivax infection (smear and PCR positive) and 34 age- and sex-matched uninfected healthy donors (controls; Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study cohort.

claim: The median peripheral parasitaemia was 4290 infected red blood cells (iRBCs)/μL of blood.
source: The median peripheral parasitaemia was 4290 infected red blood cells (iRBCs)/μL of blood (25–75 interquartile range 1860–6620 parasites/μL) and parasite load of 26,642 copies of 18S RNA/μL (25–75 interquartile range 9253–522,297).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort.

claim: 38% of P. vivax patients presented with anaemia.
source: Analysis of haematological parameters revealed significantly reduced haemoglobin levels and haematocrit across P. vivax patients compared to controls, with anaemia in 38% of the patients (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Leukocyte numbers were significantly decreased in P. vivax patients compared to controls (mean ± SD: 4.36 ± 1.74 × 103/μL vs. 5.72 ± 1.34 × 103/μL, p=0.0004).
source: Similarly, leukocyte numbers were significantly decreased (mean ± SD: 4.36 ± 1.74 × 103/μL vs. 5.72 ± 1.34 × 103/μL, p=0.0004), with 54.5% of the patients presenting with leukopenia (deﬁned as a leukocyte count <4000 cells/μL).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort with statistical analysis.

claim: 54.5% of P. vivax patients presented with leukopenia.
source: Similarly, leukocyte numbers were significantly decreased (mean ± SD: 4.36 ± 1.74 × 103/μL vs. 5.72 ± 1.34 × 103/μL, p=0.0004), with 54.5% of the patients presenting with leukopenia (deﬁned as a leukocyte count <4000 cells/μL).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort.

claim: Only 8.3% of P. vivax patients were presenting with neutropenia.
source: In contrast, neutrophil counts were not significantly different, and only 8.3% of P. vivax patients were presenting with neutropenia (neutrophil counts < 1500 cells/μL) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Monocytes, basophils, and eosinophils (MXD) were significantly reduced in P. vivax patients.
source: Other myeloid cell populations, however, such as monocytes, basophils, and eosinophils (MXD), were significantly reduced.
evidence: This is data from the study cohort.

claim: 80% of P. vivax patients presented with lymphopenia.
source: We also observed a significant reduction in lymphocyte and platelet counts in this cohort (Figure 1C), with 80% presenting with lymphopenia (lymphocyte counts < 1000 cells/μL) and 87% with thrombocytopenia (platelet counts < 150,000 cells/μL), many of them with severely reduced levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 87% of P. vivax patients presented with thrombocytopenia.
source: We also observed a significant reduction in lymphocyte and platelet counts in this cohort (Figure 1C), with 80% presenting with lymphopenia (lymphocyte counts < 1000 cells/μL) and 87% with thrombocytopenia (platelet counts < 150,000 cells/μL), many of them with severely reduced levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A significant increase in mean platelet volume was observed in P. vivax patients.
source: Alterations in platelet counts were accompanied by the release of mega platelets in the peripheral circulation as a significant increase on mean platelet volume was observed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Unsupervised clustering revealed two patient subgroups that differ in total parasite biomass but not peripheral parasitaemia.
source: Direct comparison of the two patient subgroups revealed significant higher total parasite biomass but not peripheral parasitaemia or parasite load (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Total parasite biomass was higher than and not correlated with peripheral parasitaemia levels or parasite load, particularly in patients of cluster 2.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Barber et al., 2015; Fonseca et al., 2017; Silva-Filho et al., 2021), z-score comparison further demonstrated that total parasite biomass was higher than and not correlated with peripheral parasitaemia levels or parasite load, particularly in patients of cluster 2 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 3B and C, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PvLDH was the input parasite variable with the highest loading score (correlation = 0.59) and lowest p-value (0.0000917) in the first PC dimension when compared with peripheral parasitaemia and parasite load.
source: In addition, PvLDH was the input parasite variable with the highest loading score (correlation = 0.59) and lowest p-value (0.0000917) in the first PC dimension when compared with peripheral parasitaemia and parasite load (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's PCA analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PvLDH is the best parasite predictor attribute segregating patients into clusters 1b and 2.
source: Indeed, using a best-fit classification tree model and a random forest machine learning model defining K-means clusters as categorical outcome, PvLDH is the best parasite predictor attribute segregating patients into clusters 1b and 2 (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's machine learning analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Vivaxhigh patients showed a more intense reduction in platelet counts when compared to Vivaxlow patients (Vivaxhigh 63,000 ± 6413 vs. Vivaxlow: 100,700 ± 9381; p=0.002).
source: Vivaxhigh patients showed a more intense reduction in platelet counts when compared to Vivaxlow patients (Vivaxhigh 63,000 ± 6413 vs. Vivaxlow: 100,700 ± 9381; p=0.002), with a higher frequency of patients with severe thrombocytopenia (Vivaxhigh 47% vs. Vivaxlow 8%) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 47% of Vivaxhigh patients had severe thrombocytopenia compared to 8% of Vivaxlow patients.
source: Vivaxhigh patients showed a more intense reduction in platelet counts when compared to Vivaxlow patients (Vivaxhigh 63,000 ± 6413 vs. Vivaxlow: 100,700 ± 9381; p=0.002), with a higher frequency of patients with severe thrombocytopenia (Vivaxhigh 47% vs. Vivaxlow 8%) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 88% of Vivaxhigh patients presented lymphopenia versus 64% in Vivaxlow patients.
source: Although not significant, there was a trend in the reduction of lymphocyte counts in Vivaxhigh patients when compared to Vivaxlow, with 88% of Vivaxhigh patients presenting lymphopenia versus 64% in Vivaxlow patients.
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups.

claim: There was a fourfold increase in the frequency of patients with severe lymphopenia in the Vivaxhigh cluster compared to Vivaxlow patients.
source: In addition, we observed a fourfold increase in the frequency of patients with severe lymphopenia in the Vivaxhigh cluster compared to Vivaxlow patients (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mixed cell counts (MXD) were significantly reduced in Vivaxhigh patients.
source: While there was no change in the number of circulating neutrophils in the different clusters of individuals, mixed cell counts (MXD), a parameter representing monocytes, basophils, and eosinophils numbers, were significantly reduced in Vivaxhigh patients.
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups.

claim: There was a significant enrichment of neutrophils in the leukocyte fraction in the blood of Vivaxhigh patients as well as a higher NLCR.
source: As a result, there was a significant enrichment of neutrophils in the leukocyte fraction in the blood of Vivaxhigh patients as well as a higher NLCR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Plasma levels of cytokines inducing megakaryocytic differentiation in the BM, thrombopoietin (TPO), and IL-11 were significantly increased in Vivaxhigh patients.
source: In parallel to more severe thrombocytopenia in Vivaxhigh patients, plasma levels of cytokines inducing megakaryocytic differentiation in the BM, thrombopoietin (TPO), and IL-11 were significantly increased in this cluster (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the two patient subgroups shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Vivaxhigh cluster showed a significant increase in the levels of proinflammatory cytokines associated with induction of myeloid-biased haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) differentiation and inhibition of lymphopoiesis in BM (e.g. TNF-α, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8).
source: In accordance with the pattern of immune cell fractions in the peripheral blood of P. vivax patients, the Vivaxhigh cluster showed a significant increase in the levels of proinflammatory cytokines associated with induction of myeloid-biased haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) differentiation and inhibition of lymphopoiesis in BM (e.g. TNF-α, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8; Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Boiko and Borghesi, 2012; Chiba et al., 2018; Kovtonyuk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 4C, with interpretation supported by citations to Boiko and Borghesi, 2012; Chiba et al., 2018; Kovtonyuk et al., 2016.

claim: Vivaxhigh patients had increased circulating levels of G-CSF, a major mediator of HSC-biased myelopoiesis and the neutrophil activation marker, L-selectin.
source: In addition, Vivaxhigh patients had increased circulating levels of G-CSF, a major mediator of HSC-biased myelopoiesis and the neutrophil activation marker, L-selectin (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Soehnlein et al., 2017; Ivetic, 2018; Crockett-Torabi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort shown in Figure 4C, with interpretation supported by citations to Soehnlein et al., 2017; Ivetic, 2018; Crockett-Torabi et al., 1995.

claim: Circulating levels of EC adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, and P-selectin) and other EC activation markers and procoagulant molecules (Ang-2, VWF-A2, CD40L, and PAI-1) were significantly increased in the plasma of Vivaxhigh patients compared to Vivaxlow patients and healthy controls.
source: In our cohort, circulating levels of EC adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, and P-selectin) and other EC activation markers and procoagulant molecules (Ang-2, VWF-A2, CD40L, and PAI-1) were significantly increased in the plasma of Vivaxhigh patients compared to Vivaxlow patients and healthy controls (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the patient subgroups shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Syndecan-1, a marker of EC glycocalyx breakdown, was significantly increased in Vivaxhigh but not in Vivaxlow patients.
source: Likewise, Syndecan-1, a marker of EC glycocalyx breakdown (i.e. damage of EC plasma membrane; Yeo et al., 2019; Pillinger and Kam, 2017), was significantly increased in Vivaxhigh but not in Vivaxlow patients (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is data from the study cohort comparing the patient subgroups shown in Figure 5A, with interpretation supported by citations to Yeo et al., 2019; Pillinger and Kam, 2017.

claim: Only pooled plasma from Vivaxhigh patients induces significant transcriptional upregulation of EC activation markers ICAM-1, IL-1α, and IL-8 along with downregulation of Ang-1, ADAMTS13, and NOS3 (eNOS) in HUVECs.
source: These experiments demonstrated that only pooled plasma from Vivaxhigh patients induces significant transcriptional upregulation of EC activation markers ICAM-1, IL-1α, and IL-8 along with downregulation of Ang-1, ADAMTS13, and NOS3 (eNOS) in HUVECs (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is data from ex vivo experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Flow cytometry and immunofluorescence assays revealed increased prevalence and protein expression levels of EC activation markers ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 upon exposure with Vivaxhigh pooled plasma.
source: In contrast, flow cytometry and immunofluorescence assays performed with stimulated HUVECs revealed increased prevalence and protein expression levels of EC activation markers ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 upon exposure with Vivaxhigh pooled plasma (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), in support of qRT-PCR data.
evidence: This is data from ex vivo experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The network analysis revealed a decentralized topology, lower complexity and connectivity between the edges with data from P. vivax patients compared to the highly dense, homogenous and centralized network graph of healthy donors (91 edges vs. 166 edges, respectively).
source: The network analysis revealed a decentralized topology, lower complexity and connectivity between the edges with data from P. vivax patients compared to the highly dense, homogenous and centralized network graph of healthy donors (91 edges vs. 166 edges, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's network analysis.

claim: PvLDH connects the two main functional modules 1 and 2 in the network graph of P. vivax patients.
source: Most notably, PvLDH connects the two main functional modules 1 and 2 (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's network analysis shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: PvLDH has high significant and positive associations with multiple host parameters, including Syndecan-1 (EC damage), VCAM-1, VWF (EC activation and platelet pooling), and IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α (inflammation and myelopoiesis-inducing cytokines).
source: Accordingly with Figures 2, 6A and B, the biological significance of total parasite biomass, but not peripheral parasitaemia or parasite load, in affecting host response is also corroborated by the high significant and positive associations of PvLDH with multiple host parameters, including Syndecan-1 (EC damage), VCAM-1, VWF (EC activation and platelet pooling), and IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α (inflammation and myelopoiesis-inducing cytokines) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Platelet, lymphocyte, and neutrophil counts are negatively correlated with high significance (p-value<0.0001) with total parasite biomass, but not with peripheral parasitaemia or parasite load.
source: Meanwhile, platelet, lymphocyte, and neutrophil counts are negatively correlated with high significance (p-value<0.0001) with total parasite biomass, but not with peripheral parasitaemia or parasite load (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Syndecan-1, IL-6, and platelet counts are the most dominant predictor attributes capable of classifying P. vivax patients based on total parasite biomass levels.
source: Similar to Figure 2E, application of a best-fit classification tree model demonstrated that Syndecan-1, IL-6, and platelet counts are the most dominant predictor attributes capable of classifying P. vivax patients based on total parasite biomass levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's machine learning analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PvLDH is a relevant predictor attribute (high information gain) in predicting thrombocytopenia severity, and it is associated with increased severity of thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia in the cohort.
source: In turn, PvLDH is a relevant predictor attribute (high information gain) in predicting thrombocytopenia severity, and it is associated with increased severity of thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia in our cohort (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's machine learning analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: Total parasite biomass as measured by PvLDH is a better predictor of P. vivax host responses and pathogenesis than peripheral parasitaemia.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Barber et al., 2015; Silva-Filho et al., 2021), our observations further suggest that total parasite biomass as measured by PvLDH is a better predictor of P. vivax host responses and pathogenesis than peripheral parasitaemia.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analysis, supported by citations to Barber et al., 2015 and Silva-Filho et al., 2021.

claim: The ratio of plasma pLDH to peripheral parasitaemia is sixfold higher in P. vivax-infected patients with complicated outcomes than in non-severe patients.
source: First, the discrepancy between PvLDH levels and peripheral parasitaemia determined by blood smears is more evident in P. vivax-infected patients with complicated outcomes: the ratio of plasma pLDH to peripheral parasitaemia is sixfold higher than in non-severe patients.
evidence: This is a statement based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: The same comparison between severe and non-severe P. falciparum patients reveals only a 1.4-fold difference in the ratio of plasma pLDH to peripheral parasitaemia.
source: The same comparison between severe and non-severe P. falciparum patients reveals only a 1.4-fold difference (Barber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to Barber et al., 2015.

claim: Thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia have been associated with severe manifestations and the need for blood and platelet transfusions in severe vivax malaria.
source: Second, although thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia are not included in the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for defining severe malaria, it has been associated with severe manifestations and the need for blood and platelet transfusions in severe vivax malaria.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about malaria complications.

claim: Thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia could be explored as markers of severity for P. vivax.
source: This points out their clinical relevance in malaria diagnosis and treatment (Lacerda et al., 2011; Naing and Whittaker, 2018; Gerardin et al., 2002; Kochar et al., 2010; Kochar et al., 2005), suggesting that these haematological complications could be explored as markers of severity for this species.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on inference from the study's findings and supported by citations.

claim: Elevated EC activation and damage in VivaxHigh patients results in increased cytoadherence of P. vivax iRBCs and hence accumulation and growth in deep tissues, thus reducing the fraction of the parasite biomass in circulation.
source: We hypothesize that elevated endothelial activation and damage in VivaxHigh patients results in increased cytoadherence of P. vivax iRBCs and hence accumulation and growth in deep tissues, thus reducing the fraction of the parasite biomass in circulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Elevated endothelial activation and glycocalyx damage increases the exposure of adhesion molecules, which in turn favours endothelial cytoadherence of P. vivax-infected RBCs, particularly in the splenic red pulp cords and in the BM.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Yeo et al., 2019; Barber et al., 2021), we propose that elevated EC activation and glycocalyx damage increases the exposure of adhesion molecules, which in turn favours endothelial cytoadherence of P. vivax-infected RBCs, particularly in the splenic red pulp cords and in the BM (Kho et al., 2021a; Introini et al., 2018; Hempel et al., 2017; Toda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the study's findings and supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: Syndecan-1 is a putative host biomarker (EC glycocalyx breakdown marker) predicting total parasite biomass in P. vivax patients.
source: Accordingly, application of a best-fit classification tree model identifies Syndecan-1 as a putative host biomarker (EC glycocalyx breakdown marker) predicting total parasite biomass in P. vivax patients.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's machine learning analysis.

claim: Peripheral parasitaemia is a poor predictor of clinical outcomes in P. vivax-infected individuals.
source: In contrast to P. falciparum-infected individuals, a wide range of complicated clinical syndromes occur in P. vivax patients even at low or subpatent parasitaemia (Baird, 2013), thus indicating that peripheral parasitaemia is a poor predictor of clinical outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citation to Baird, 2013.

claim: Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain the damage or excessive removal of platelets in P. vivax infection, including oxidative stress, platelet phagocytosis, IgG binding to platelet-bound malaria antigens, spleen pooling, or increased circulating nucleic acids levels.
source: Various mechanisms have been proposed to explain the damage or excessive removal of platelets in P. vivax infection, including oxidative stress, platelet phagocytosis, IgG binding to platelet-bound malaria antigens, spleen pooling, or increased circulating nucleic acids levels (Lacerda et al., 2011; Naing and Whittaker, 2018; Kochar et al., 2010; Andrade et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: EC activation and damage plays a role in intravascular platelet agglutination and increased platelet clearance from the circulation.
source: EC activation and damage also plays a role in intravascular platelet agglutination and increased platelet clearance from the circulation (Park et al., 2003; Punnath et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to Park et al., 2003 and Punnath et al., 2019.

claim: The relatively large drop in peripheral lymphocyte numbers observed in the P. vivax patients is likely non-specific effect, for example, pooling in the enlarged spleen rather than a response by Plasmodium-specific lymphocytes.
source: In contrast, the relatively large drop in peripheral lymphocyte numbers we observed in the P. vivax patients is likely non-specific effect, for example, pooling in the enlarged spleen rather than a response by Plasmodium-specific lymphocytes (Hviid and Kemp, 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by citation to Hviid and Kemp, 2000.

claim: P. vivax elicits a stronger inﬂammatory response and more pronounced endothelial activation when compared with other Plasmodium infections with similar or higher peripheral parasitaemia.
source: P. vivax elicits a stronger inﬂammatory response and more pronounced endothelial activation when compared with other Plasmodium infections with similar or higher peripheral parasitaemia (Yeo et al., 2010); however, the role of EC activation in P. vivax pathogenesis is not yet understood.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citation to Yeo et al., 2010.

claim: Damage of the EC plasma membrane, as represented by glycocalyx breakdown, has been associated with poor prognostic outcome in P. falciparum.
source: Damage of the EC plasma membrane, as represented by glycocalyx breakdown, has been associated with poor prognostic outcome in P. falciparum (Yeo et al., 2019), but there is no data available for P. vivax.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citation to Yeo et al., 2019.

claim: Soluble EC activation biomarkers (e.g. ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, Ang-2, CD40L, vWF-A2) and the EC damage product, Syndecan-1, are positively correlated with thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, anaemia, and neutrophil enrichment in the peripheral blood in the study cohort.
source: In our cohort, soluble EC activation biomarkers (e.g. ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, Ang-2, CD40L, vWF-A2) and the EC damage product, Syndecan-1, are positively correlated with thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, anaemia, and neutrophil enrichment in the peripheral blood.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: These biomarkers are positively correlated with increased circulating levels of cytokines inducing megakaryocyte differentiation (e.g. IL-11 and TPO) and with cytokines inducing myeloid-biased HSC differentiation (e.g. TNF-α, IL1-α, IL6, IL-8, and G-CSF).
source: In addition, these biomarkers are positively correlated with increased circulating levels of cytokines inducing megakaryocyte differentiation (e.g. IL-11 and TPO) and with cytokines inducing myeloid-biased HSC differentiation (e.g. TNF-α, IL1-α, IL6, IL-8, and G-CSF), suggesting both direct and indirect links between EC activation and damage and haematological perturbations.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's correlation analysis.

claim: Total parasite biomass-inducing EC activation might act synergistically with inflammatory changes potentially leading to splenic platelet pooling and platelet clumping in the vasculature without DIC.
source: Total parasite biomass-inducing EC activation might act synergistically with inflammatory changes potentially leading to splenic platelet pooling and platelet clumping in the vasculature without DIC (Lacerda et al., 2008; Pillinger and Kam, 2017; Becker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by citations.

claim: Increased activation-induced cell death (AICD) in T cells, splenic T-cell accumulation, or decreased lymphopoiesis due to myeloid-biased HSC differentiation induced by inflammatory cytokines and EC activation in the BM might explain the severe lymphopenia and neutrophilia in vivax patients.
source: Likewise, increased activation-induced cell death (AICD) in T cells, splenic T-cell accumulation (Hviid and Kemp, 2000), or decreased lymphopoiesis due to myeloid-biased HSC differentiation induced by inflammatory cytokines and EC activation in the BM (Boiko and Borghesi, 2012; Chiba et al., 2018; Silva-Filho et al., 2021) might explain the severe lymphopenia and neutrophilia in vivax patients.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by citations.

claim: The mixture of parasite and host factors in plasma can directly induce EC activation in the absence of parasitized RBCs.
source: In a second series of experiments, we performed ex vivo stimulation of HUVECs with the plasma of the P. vivax cohort demonstrating that the mixture of parasite and host factors can directly induce EC activation in the absence of parasitized RBCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's ex vivo experiments.

claim: Functional differences between HUVECs and adult vascular endothelium, including lack of ABO blood group antigen expression, have been reported.
source: Of note, functional differences between HUVECs and adult vascular endothelium, including lack of ABO blood group antigen expression, have been reported (O'Donnell et al., 2000; Tan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to O'Donnell et al., 2000 and Tan et al., 2004.

claim: ECs are capable of responding to pathogens by sensing pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs).
source: ECs are capable of responding to pathogens by sensing pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through pattern-recognition receptors (PRRs), which might play a key role in inducing EC activation when detecting P. vivax molecules enriched in the tissues where the parasite accumulates.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about EC biology.

claim: ECs express specific cytokine/chemokine receptors to detect proinﬂammatory signals released systemically or locally by activated immune cells in response to infection.
source: ECs also express specific cytokine/chemokine receptors to detect proinﬂammatory signals released systemically or locally by activated immune cells in response to infection (Bernardo et al., 2004; Bevilacqua, 1993).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to Bernardo et al., 2004 and Bevilacqua, 1993.

claim: EC activation induces exocytosis of secretory granules known as Weibel–Palade bodies that leads to the release of Ang-2 and VWF, as well as transcriptional programmes that activate expression of adhesion molecules such as ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, and secreted cytokines and chemokines.
source: As a result, EC activation induces exocytosis of secretory granules known as Weibel–Palade bodies that leads to the release of Ang-2 and VWF, as well as transcriptional programmes that activate expression of adhesion molecules such as ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, and secreted cytokines and chemokines (de Mast et al., 2007; Bernardo et al., 2004; Bevilacqua, 1993).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Systemic increase of markers of EC activation and damage was only detected in Vivaxhigh patients.
source: Our Luminex data clearly confirm such heterogeneity in the spectrum of EC changes due to P. vivax infection, with systemic increase of markers of EC activation and damage only detected in Vivaxhigh patients.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's Luminex analysis.

claim: Systemic inflammatory responses in P. vivax patients can lead to local EC activation but not vascular damage.
source: These data indicate that systemic inflammatory responses in P. vivax patients can lead to local EC activation but not vascular damage, central events in malaria pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's ex vivo experimental findings.

claim: Extracellular vesicles (EV) originating from ECs, platelets, and RBCs are present during malaria infection and are known to modulate the host immune response to the parasite.
source: It is likely that other circulating factors that we have not directly measured in our study are also contributing to EC activation and vascular permeability. In particular, extracellular vesicles (EV) originating from ECs, platelets, and RBCs are present during malaria infection and are known to modulate the host immune response to the parasite (Toda et al., 2020; Mantel et al., 2016; Mantel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to Toda et al., 2020; Mantel et al., 2016; Mantel et al., 2013.

claim: In P. falciparum, infected RBCs release EVs containing immunogenic parasite antigens, which activate macrophages, induce neutrophil migration, and alter endothelial barrier function.
source: In P. falciparum, infected RBCs release EVs containing immunogenic parasite antigens, which activate macrophages, induce neutrophil migration, and alter endothelial barrier function (Mantel et al., 2016; Mantel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to Mantel et al., 2016 and Mantel et al., 2013.

claim: In P. vivax, plasma-derived EVs from iRBCs are taken up by human spleen ﬁbroblasts (hSFs), which signals NF-kB translocation and upregulation of ICAM-1 expression, facilitating cytoadherence of P. vivax-infected reticulocytes.
source: In P. vivax, plasma-derived EVs from iRBCs are taken up by human spleen ﬁbroblasts (hSFs). This event signals NF-kB translocation and upregulation of ICAM-1 expression, facilitating cytoadherence of P. vivax-infected reticulocytes (Toda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citation to Toda et al., 2020.

claim: Patients presenting with a strong host response during acute infection might be at increased risk of deteriorating and developing severe symptoms after commencement of treatment.
source: Patients presenting with a strong host response during acute infection might therefore be at increased risk of deteriorating and developing severe symptoms after commencement of treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Identification of unique biological signatures in P. vivax patients might help to build rational approaches to the diagnosis, prognosis, and individualized treatment to modulate the host response to vivax malaria.
source: Thus, identification of unique biological signatures in P. vivax patients might help to build rational approaches to the diagnosis, prognosis, and individualized treatment to modulate the host response to vivax malaria.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the implications of the study's findings.

claim: Changes in clinical parameters and biomarkers detected in the plasma of P. vivax patients are the result of both systemic host responses and local infection in tissue reservoirs such as BM and spleen.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that changes in clinical parameters and biomarkers detected in the plasma of P. vivax patients are the result of both systemic host responses and local infection in tissue reservoirs such as BM and spleen.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analysis.

claim: Measuring a combination of host parameters (e.g. Syndecan-1, IL-6, platelet levels) and total parasite biomass (PvLDH) could predict the extent of parasite infection outside of circulation.
source: Our analysis shows that measuring a combination of host parameters (e.g. Syndecan-1, IL-6, platelet levels) and total parasite biomass (PvLDH) could predict the extent of parasite infection outside of circulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's machine learning analysis.

claim: PvLDH is produced by viable or recently killed parasites and hence considered a proxy for ongoing rather than past infection.
source: PvLDH is produced by viable or recently killed parasites and hence considered a proxy for ongoing rather than past infection (Barber et al., 2015; Druilhe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citations to Barber et al., 2015 and Druilhe et al., 2007.

claim: PvLDH antigen capture ELISA established a direct relationship between pLDH levels and P. vivax parasitaemia in ex vivo experiments.
source: PvLDH antigen capture ELISA established a direct relationship between pLDH levels and P. vivax parasitaemia in ex vivo experiments, demonstrating that pLDH reflects total P. vivax parasite biomass (Druilhe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge supported by citation to Druilhe et al., 2007.
